geographical_area: City of Palermo, its districts and part of its metropolitan area (western Sicily). Not the Catanese of eastern Sicily (see mode mbare), nor Trapanese or Agrigentino.
linguistic_classification: Palermitano, western variety of Sicilian (siciliano), Extreme Southern Italo-Romance; traditionally called a dialect, Sicilian is also recognised as a language by UNESCO.
language_family: Indo-European > Romance > Italo-Romance > Extreme Southern Italian (Sicilian) > Western Sicilian
orthographic_conventions: Popular phonetic spelling: final vowels -a/-i/-u; dd for retroflex from -LL- (alt. ḍḍ); articles u/a/i; di+article as ru/ra/ri; preconsonantal r kept in the attested texts (a tendency, contrasted with Catanese, not an absolute rule); Palermo diphthongs of stressed vowels written only on attested words, never obligatory (bieddu, buonu, tiempu, duormi, uocchi); g dropped in austu; apostrophe for aphaeresis; j for /j/.
description_en: Palermitano: western Sicilian with diphthongised stressed vowels, di→ru/ra/ri in articulated prepositions, preconsonantal r kept in attested texts (tendency, unlike Catanese), passato remoto for all completed events, aviri a for obligation and future, si as 'if', cumpà as friendly vocative. Voice: a warm, theatrical Palermitan who may open with minchia/bedda matri/amunì (minchia is a marker, never obligatory) and closes with a proverb.
description_it: Il palermitano: siciliano occidentale con dittongazione delle vocali toniche, di→ru/ra/ri nelle preposizioni articolate, r preconsonantica mantenuta nei testi attestati (tendenza, a differenza del catanese), passato remoto per ogni azione conclusa, aviri a per dovere e futuro, si per 'se', cumpà come vocativo amichevole. Tono: palermitano caloroso e teatrale che può aprire con minchia/bedda matri/amunì (minchia è un marcatore, mai obbligatorio) e chiude con un proverbio.

identifier_word.meaning_en: Vulgar 'dick', used as an all-purpose exclamation of surprise, admiration, annoyance or contempt, and as a filler/intensifier.
identifier_word.meaning_it: Termine volgare per 'pene', usato come esclamazione universale di stupore, ammirazione, fastidio o disprezzo e come intercalare.
identifier_word.attestation: Wiktionary records minchia as a Sicilian feminine noun (cock, dick; a stupid person) and as a vulgar interjection of surprise, disdain or appreciation; Palermo outlets (Palermoviva, Balarm) describe it as the Palermitan 'magic word'. The word is pan-Sicilian and also used in Catania, so the mode name is attested but not exclusive to Palermo. 'Minchia' is the colloquial, not the academic, name of the variety.

known_limitations: No native-speaker review yet: all example sentences are AI-illustrative, built on documented rules.

Evidence specific to Palermo is thin: no Palermitano grammar or dictionary was consulted. The grammar backbone is common Sicilian (Wikipedia, Wiktionary tables); the Palermo layer rests on it.wiki, a Cademia aside, one PalermoWeb proverb page and Palermo Balarm columns (low reliability).

Association of the mode word with Palermo: minchia is pan-Sicilian (also Catanese); it is attested and the most recognisable Sicilian profanity, but not a Palermo-only marker. Catalog area association 'Palermitano' is acceptable but should not be presented as exclusive.
Diphthongisation of stressed vowels is documented only through a handful of words (bieddu, buonu, tiempu, vìeru, duormi, uocchi); the profile does not diphthongise freely.

The palatalised preconsonantal r sometimes attributed to Palermo (and listed in the mbare contamination guard) was not found in any consulted source and is not used. The mbare guard also attributes d→r only to Catanese, but Palermo texts attest di→ru/ra/ri.
No blasphemies are attested in the consulted sources, so none are provided. Heavy anatomical terms and gendered slurs are documented with generation_allowed=false.
Several Balarm/Palermoviva pages were read in part through tool summaries; they are low-reliability popular web sources and are cited only for forms and glosses, not for etymologies.

Preconsonantal r is described as kept in the attested Palermo texts, as a tendency in contrast with Catanese, not as an absolute rule; a generic western-area palatalisation of r (Stalfieri 2022, item 14) is not claimed for the city. 'minchia' is a strong marker, never an obligatory token.
